units.text: Growing Trees of Culture
Using Appreciative Inquiry and embodied placemaking as strategies for self-regulation inside the conservatoire
A N D R E A L . M O O R A N D J E R E M Y N E I D E C K W I T H J E A N E T T E F A B I L A A N D M A R G I B R O W N A S H I N T R O D U C T I O N

Across the Australian higher education landscape fault lines are emerging between institutions that are questioning the viability and sustainability of the conservatoire, and academic staff who are committed to maintaining excellence in actor training (Moor 2021).The COVID-induced digital pivot has led to greater flexibility in teaching modes and heavier reliance on independent practice (Pike et al. 2020), leading to a destabilization and recalibration of the power dynamics of actor/ director and student/teacher (Neideck et al. 2021).As the cultural and creative industries seek stability in the wake of the powerful aftershocks of #MeToo and #BlackLivesMatter, there has been a rush to develop policies aimed at reducing abuses of power and encouraging healthy and productive ways of being in the workplace (Park and Neideck 2020).In the fastpaced, embodied and emotionally vulnerable environment of the actor's studio however, the distribution and dissemination of formal guidelines regarding behavioural norms is often perceived as counterproductive, or as frustrating to individual creativity.This paper outlines ways in which Appreciative Inquiry is employed in collaboration with forms of embodied placemaking facilitated by full-time staff and artists in Queensland University of Technology's actor training programme.These strategies are used to model respectful relationships; to empower cohorts of student actors to negotiate boundaries of consent and outline their own behavioural expectations and to enable academics to provide continuity of care in uncertain times.Observations will be made regarding the ways in which these rituals of practice and living policies shift and change over time, constituting not 'a legal document', but 'a cultural document' (Fischer and Myers 2017).These strategies enable ensembles to self-regulate and are used to navigate the tricky intermediate space between the conservatoire and industry.
C O N T E X T : I N S T I T U T I O N A L F A U L T L I N E S A N D T H E S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y O F T H E C O N S E R V A T O I R E

Since the outbreak of COVID-19 and the resultant social and economic insecurity, higher education institutions around the world have either been forced or have chosen to make drastic cuts to performing arts programmes.As Julian Meyrick (2021) has observed, Australia has recently seen the closure of five university drama departments and the scaling back of another three with programmes that have survived being forced to reduce student contact hours, limit their reliance on casual teaching staff and guest artists and increase the volume of studentled activity.Academic staff are increasingly forced to comply with government mandates and institutional guidelines while trying to support the student body as they angst over perceptions of the erosion of the quality of their programmes.et al. 2020).
C A L L F O R C H A N G E : # B L A C K L I V E S M A T T E R A N D T H E A N T I - R A C I S T T U R N

In the UK this resulted in the formation of the Race Equality Consultants group, an offshoot of the Equity Race Equality Committee (Masso 2020), set up to advise drama schools, many of whom were criticized for their lack of racial awareness and outdated teaching practices.This has brought into question the validity of the Euro-centric conservatoire system and forced educators to look to different models of learning (Moor 2021).The traditional format of the conservatoire centres long hours of intensive training led by a master teacher, a mode that reinforces the power dynamic of master and apprentice.Many non-European methods of cultural sharing, however, focus on the communal building of understanding through rituals of practice, allowing a circular experience where diverse forms of creativity are respected (Luckett and Shaffer 2017).An important aspect of Australian Indigenous culture is the yarning circle, a space for all to sit within and listen and share in turn.Nauiyu elder, artist and educator Miriam Rose Ungunmerr-Baumann stresses the importance of this kind of 'deep listening' as a process of silent, still awareness of one another and the land on which we live (2002).This circularly democratic process of sharing and listening leans more on the importance of process over outcome.

If we consider a Western mode of learning as allowing the teacher 'as expert' to act within a master-apprentice relationship, then we might consider alternative modes such as yarning to be a 'circular' experience.The masterapprentice model tends to 'privilege the power and voice of the lecturer-practitioner above the student' (Seton and Trouton 2014), and when teachers are not representative of the cultural background of the students there is a greater chance of students feeling ill at ease or 'unsafe' within this power structure.The embedding of embodied and circular processes of placemaking as explored within the QUT Acting Orientation week experience attempts to provide a safer space for all students, especially those of diverse cultural backgrounds, and establish a model for power negotiation within the student cohort.
C A L L F O R C H A N G E : # M E T O O A N D S A F E T H E A T R E P R A C T I C E

The #MeToo movement, which rose to public consciousness in 2018, highlighted the abuses of power experienced, particularly by women, in all areas of the film and theatre industries (Park and Neideck 2020).Across the world, theatre companies and unions looked to develop measures for safer theatre practice, and many modelled their approaches on the ground-breaking work undertaken by Lori Myers and Laura T. Fisher in the development of the Chicago Theatre Standards (CTS) in 2015.Intimacy on stage and screen is now safeguarded with the employment of specialist intimacy directors in many countries around the world, and it has become commonplace for screen and theatre producers to hire intimacy directors to support such work.The #MeToo campaign brought to light systemic abuses of power in the film and theatre industries, resulting in the institution of processes and protocols to safeguard against bullying, harassment of all kinds and discrimination.In Australia this saw a coming together of artists, theatre administrators and training institutions to develop guidelines for safe theatre practices at several national safe theatre practice conferences.Training institutions, theatre and screen peak bodies have all adopted policies that clearly outline acceptable behaviour with clear lines of reporting of abuse of power.Further to these protocols, many companies worldwide are expanding these guidelines to include cultural statements.For example, in November 2020, Sydney Theatre Company published a Cultural Representation Pledge in which they committed to greater representation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander and culturally and linguistically diverse artists and storytelling.The statement also commits to engaging processes of dramaturgy other than that influenced by the Western canon with a commitment to honouring playmaking processes in line with the culture of the playwright.Such measures are not only influencing major change in our cultural outputs but are also helping to safeguard the mental health of all theatre artists.Organizations such as the Arts Wellbeing Collective, based at the Melbourne Arts Centre, are providing support to all theatre workers in maintaining strong mental health protocols while working in cities and on tour.Arts organizations and training institutions in the UK have been encouraged by the Revolution or Nothing Network to consider their stance as the Black and Global Majority in ending systemic racism (2020).

S I T U A T I N G T H E C A S E S T U D Y : T H E
Q U T A C T I N G E N V I R O N M E N T

For many years QUT Acting has been one of the leading actor training programmes in Australia with particularly strong emphasis on training for screen.Over the last five years the programme has sought to align with the objectives of the Queensland University of Technology Blueprint (2019), which in its various iterations has always highlighted the need for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander perspectives to sit at the core of what we do.Programme facilitators have looked at how these perspectives can be applied in a meaningful and impactful way.Far from tokenistic, the Orientation Week activity sets up the groundwork for not only a more inclusive culture but lays the foundation for a horizontal hierarchy of learning that places the importance on the ensemble rather than the individual.Samantha Slade believes that humans are non-hierarchical creatures and that we become engaged when working together in a non-hierarchical environment, proposing that we tend to disengage when autonomy is taken from us (2018).The process of theatre and screen creation is a team engagement and actors must know what it is to be part of a team, to support other members of a team and to want to excel with, and for, the team.This philosophy also assists in creating artists who may choose to extend their practice beyond acting by embracing other elements of the theatre-/ screen-making process.

Our experience has resonances with those of our colleagues at Toi Whakaari, the New Zealand Drama School, who, well before the constraints of COVID-19, were pushing many training facilities to adapt and change, set about de-colonizing their curriculum and building a bi-cultural programme that embraced both Māori and Western European approaches.By embracing Indigenous perspectives, staff at that institution have been able to adapt traditional modes to best suit each student's development (Moor 2021).• Be impeccable with your words.

These agreements set up principles for living that apply particularly well to building a cohesive ensemble, and also underpin the teaching of collaboration and devised performance in QUT's School of Creative Practice (Neideck 2018).
ARTICULATING GROUP NORMS AND ENSEMBLE VALUES IN THE QUT ACTING PROGRAMME

As outlined in our introduction, arts and cultural institutions around the world have responded to the current social moment with various codes, frameworks and strategies for the governing of human behaviour and relationships -what Choi Dai-Kwon (2004) has described as formalized intermediate norms, 'ethical codes of conduct regulating intermediate areas of human activities between the law and individual choice' (92).For many years, the discipline areas of acting, drama and technical production at QUT circulated formalized intermediate norms in the form of a handbook that articulated institutional knowledge and professional expectations as understood by the faculty's teaching staff.However, without mechanisms of regular maintenance and review, this handbook became an increasingly inefficient instrument of instruction.In recent years, a new approach became necessary.

Establishing foundational processes of inclusion and autonomy were deemed the best way to create a 'culture' of inclusion and support within the QUT Acting student cohorts.Brown Ash begins this process by setting up the 'group norms' or 'contract of engagement' with students using her RICC process, allowing students to live up to their individual values while maintaining a strong sense of ensemble throughout their training journey.These group norms are developed through improvisation and group work and allow everyone to speak to their own values and highlight issues that matter to them.They have proven to be an effective tool of self-determination and students are encouraged to refer to them when addressing interpersonal issues and tensions within the ensemble.Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (2014) claims that creativity is informed by one's background and that the success of that creativity depends on the audience of it.He asserts that a creative domain prescribes the criteria for appraisal of that creativity.The domain of an actor training institution is shaped by those teaching within it and therefore the creative output of students is deemed successful from this lens.The shifting of this hierarchy of appraisal to one of communal support and regard allows for the unbiased development of the student's abilities.

Once this foundational work is established, Neideck has worked with the students throughout their first year to articulate their group norms as a set of ensemble values, a form of 'living policy' (Fischer and Myers 2017) that shifts and changes over time.Neideck's approach to creating this document is to work as a facilitator and scribe of useful discussion at crucial milestones throughout the year, and at points where individual or ensemble issues arise.Using the Appreciative Inquiry principles of discovering what is working well in a system, dreaming how the future can be brighter and designing steps for getting there (after Cooperrider and Whitney 2005), this process is supported by the setting of regular assessment tasks that encourage the development of Hatton and Smith's standards of critical reflection (1995), the demonstration of an awareness that actions and events are not only located in and explained by multiple perspectives, but that they are influenced by multiple historical and sociopolitical contexts (61-2).

The Ensemble Norms and Values that emerge out of this process become an important touchstone -a tool for shared accountability.Through their process of development, students experience a sense of the horizontal power structure that staff in the acting programme set out to emulate.Similar to the Montessori philosophy of education (Montessori, Hunt and Valsiner 2014), students within QUT Acting are encouraged to advance at their own pace with teachers acting as 'guides' rather than 'master', as is common in the conservatoire system.This shift is also described by Loth and Neideck (2022) as an expression of what Mather and Hulme (2013) have called a transformation of the Performance Model or striving for an 'externally established standard' to that of a Mastery Model, or 'a desire to learn for the sake of increasing knowledge' (56).Students are also encouraged to adopt a leadership mindset, using the guiding principles of the group norms to lead any process, rather than relying on a teacher to do so.

M O O R A N D N E I D E C K W I T H F A B I LA A N D A S H : G R O W I N G T R E E S O F C U LT U R E

The group norms and ensemble values articulated by students are very often aspirational, and sometimes reach outside of the domains in which they and teaching staff can apply influence, however, where practical and appropriate, full-time staff attempt to help students to fulfil them.For example, the mentoring of first-year students by those more advanced in their study; the encouragement of students to work on their own personal goals, aside from university grades; disengagement from competition and comparison between students; and the facilitation of training and activities across year-level cohorts, allowing students to learn from and challenge one another.One of the most significant opportunities for this is in the QUT Acting Full Company Yarning.
Q U T A C T I N G ' S F U L L C O M P A N Y Y A R N I N G

The QUT Acting Full Company Yarning is an activity undertaken during Orientation Week designed to bring all three cohort year groups of Acting students together to welcome the first-year students into the university and, more importantly, into the culture of the acting programme.This activity of 'deep listening' (Ungunmerr-Baumann 2002) helps to immediately set expectations that the culture of QUT Acting is one of empathy, belonging and respect, acknowledging the colonized history of Australia and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people.

The students initially sit in a circle, joined by Moor, Neideck, Fabila and Brown Ash.Mention is made that the space we are holding is one of respect, and after each of the facilitators is briefly introduced, Aunty Jeanette leads an Acknowledgement of Country.In Australian civic life, it has become increasingly customary for an Acknowledgement of Country to be given in circumstances when a Traditional Owner or Custodian is not available to deliver a Welcome to Country.Although there is no national protocol for acknowledging the Traditional Owners or Custodians of Country, it is customary to pay respects to them and to Elders past and present and to acknowledge the traditional use of the land on which the gathering is taking place (National Indigenous Australians Agency n.d.).She explains to students the importance of the inclusion of an Acknowledgement of Country to bring the spirits of the land into the work that we do.This process also helps bridge us into an ecological approach to art making and reminds us of the resilience of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in the face of Australia's violent histories of colonization.Jeanette then leads the group in the performance of the Ochre Dance, an embodied Acknowledgement of Country that she has developed, and that we will explain further below.
B U I L D I N G T H E T R E E O F C U L T U R E

We then set up the process for constructing our Tree of Culture, which is the central artefact that guides the rest of the session, with each activity designed to contribute to the formation of the Tree's roots, trunk, branches and leaves.

First are the roots.Aunty Jeanette explains how participating in a ritual of naming our ancestry and our connections to Country calls in our own ancestors, spirits and histories.Brown Ash invites the students to write their name and any key words that describe their identity on a paper root as they gather their thoughts before sharing.Commencing students receive a blank root, while continuing students are invited to contemplate the roots saved from the previous year.Each individual is then invited to share: the name they wish to be known by, the pronouns they use and their connection to Country, nature or home.Aunty Jeanette encourages each person to take their time to follow the practice of the 'patient sharing of voices', something that she identifies with Indigenous processes of sharing space.Once everyone has completed this activity, they are all invited to place their roots in the centre of the circle, allowing to grow the trunk and branches.
The trunk of the tree is developed through o Own your slip-ups if they happen.o There is no requirement to disclose your personal experiences in or out of the studio.

a group discussion as Brown Ash and Aunty Jeanette ask students to share their impressions of what it means to create a culture together.Ideas and concepts are scribed onto the paper trunk and added to the roots already in place.

The branches of the tree are derived from small group discussions.Each facilitator works with a group, encouraging the secondand third-year students to take the lead in a discussion based on principles of appreciation and dreaming, recording the main points on paper branches.Prompts central to the initial stages of the Appreciative Inquiry process include questions such as 'What is going well?' or 'What gives you life?' in the programme and what is the best of what QUT Acting has to offer.First-year students are encouraged to dream, putting into words what they are dreaming of, what they are looking forward to and what their greatest expectations are for their time in the programme.These words are shared with the whole group as the branches are placed around the trunk.
Finally, Brown Ash encourages each person to write down any thoughts or reflections on the words they are hearing.These form the leaves, which are then added to complete the Tree of Culture.
A B O R I G I N A L A N D T O R R E S S T R A I T I S L A N D E R M O D E S O F P L A C E M A K I N G

Aunty Jeanette believes that the acknowledgement of each person's connection to Country puts everyone on the same page and facilitates the creation of an environment of respect for all.It is tradition for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples to acknowledge the Country that they are visiting, and as a touring performer Aunty Jeanette considers this ritual not only a sign of respect but a vital workplace health and safety protocol.She always tells the ancestors of whatever Country that she visits that she is arriving and that she is leaving, to make sure that her spirit leaves with her.Asking non-Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander students to acknowledge the local name for the land that they have come from, as well as sharing information about their own cultural heritage, helps offer a bridge into this perspective for the first time.This form of universal acknowledgement helps all involved gain a sense of how we should all honour our heritage and respect each other's Country.The Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander students report feeling seen, and those new students are able to immediately connect with other Indigenous students.Aunty Jeanette points out that there is trauma for some as they journey to Australia, and they may be carrying the baggage of the land they have left.Even though their memory of their homeland may be fraught with civil and social unrest, it is important for them to feel that they have family here in this new land to keep the spirit of all students alive.Aunty Jeanette believes that this sharing of place assists the students in appreciating the difference between Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures, and their own culture.That inclusive 'bringing of self' to the work and to the group is quite different to how many traditional conservatories have operated, where students may be told to 'leave your baggage at the door'.Aunty Jeanette reflected on how this attitude was a limit to her ability in ballet school, embedding patterns of tension in her body when relaxation would have helped her to extend her technique.

The Ochre Dance, which Aunty Jeanette leads as a form of embodied Acknowledgement of Country, came to her in a dream on the night of the passing of Russell Page, Nunukul and Munaldjali man, one of the principal dancers of Bangarra Dance Theatre, and brother to the company's long-term artistic director, Stephen Page and music director and song man, David Page.Aunty Jeanette recalls that on the night of his passing, a willie wagtail (rhipidura leucophrys) appeared on her veranda trying to wake her up with the sad news.The willie wagtail is Aunty Jeanette's totem, and the presence of the bird in her surroundings always holds strong resonance for her.Russell's passing was a shock that was felt throughout communities in South-East Queensland, and Aunty Jeanette created the dance in honour of Russell and would use it to let children she worked with know that they were calling their uncle to help them with their dancing.She has since used the dance in many different contexts and has found it to have
M O O R A N D N E I D E C K W I T H F A B I LA A N D A S H : G R O W I N G T R E E S O F C U LT U R E

restorative powers, even with people who claim they can't dance.She believes that the dance connects people to Russell's land of the Nunukul people and the Munaldjali clan of the Yugambeh Nation.This powerful story of intergenerational care resonates with the dynamics of mentorship that we attempt to instil in our student actors.

The Ochre Dance is Jeanette's way of giving back to all the Elders she has learned from by acknowledging that we need to look after the four elements of fire, water, earth and wind.The dance starts with fire in honour of Russell Page's fiery spirit, with participants rubbing their hands together to generate energy.The dance moves to water, which replenishes us after fire, honouring the Rainbow Serpent who created all animals from water.From water we move into earth with the Kangaroo dance where we rub mud, the combination of water and earth, all over our bodies.The connection to totems continues with wind being represented by birds.Aunty Jeanette includes a chant throughout the dance that calls in the ancestors of all present and introduces them to the ancestors of the Country where we are working.This communal calling of all our ancestors is a natural way of acknowledging that we are all human beings.The dance forms a touchstone for the students and Aunty Jeanette believes that it helps guide the student's spirits back to their bodies.Throughout this whole process all facilitators participate, assisting in building the culture of a horizontal power dynamic.
C O N C L U S I O N : R I T U A L S O F C A R E

The work of Margi Brown Ash and Aunty Jeanette Fabila has helped to form a foundation for the culture within the QUT Acting programme.These processes of respect are then carried through to consent and intimacy discussions and workshops, outlining consent in both the studio and social spaces.It is hoped that by setting up the rules of engagement within a respectful environment students will feel confident talking about what makes them uncomfortable, including objectification, body shaming, unsolicited touch and gaze, increasing all students' awareness of their own actions in both the social and studio setting.Boundary awareness creates an environment for creativity where students can claim their own social, cultural, physical and psychological boundaries.Rituals of de-roling and leaving the work are also encouraged with appropriate support mechanisms for working on challenging content in place.

We believe that these rituals set up our students for success.We rarely see fierce competition between the students and are always comforted by the support that is freely given from one student to another.The notion of 'care' is taken very seriously above and beyond the student support offered by the university.It is important that this care is generated by the students themselves in how they work with one another and how they overcome the challenges that will arise.Mutual respect has been the aspiration of this approach and mostly we feel we have achieved this.

We live in a time of increased mental health issues, exacerbated by the fallout of the COVID-19 pandemic, and a limited staff body cannot possibly hold that level of distress as part of their daily workload.By introducing the cohort to the inclusive Orientation Week experience we aim to provide support structures within the acting student cohort.By introducing them to The Four Agreements, working with them to establish their group norms and continuing to engage in the principles of WAWPT, we are finding that students are not only able to solve issues before they come to a head but are able to create a happy and nurturing environment within which they can face all the challenges of their training.
